text: Lesson 38, Chapter 6. You've seen why a learned reward model is necessary, how preference data gets collected, and the loss it trains against. This lesson puts all three together into actual training code with Hugging Face's TRL library.

A reward model starts from a pretrained transformer, usually the same base model being aligned. The only architectural change is the output head: instead of a vocabulary-sized softmax, you swap in a single scalar unit. AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels equals one gives you exactly that — a classifier head repurposed as a scalar regression head.

RewardTrainer and RewardConfig wrap this in a familiar Hugging Face training loop. You hand it the model, standard training arguments like batch size, and a dataset of chosen-rejected pairs — exactly the preference data from two lessons ago. Call train, and it handles everything else.

Under the hood, for every pair, it tokenizes both the chosen and rejected sequence, runs both through the model to get two scalar scores, and minimizes the Bradley-Terry loss on the difference between them — pushing the model to score chosen responses higher than rejected ones.

What comes out is a single scalar scorer that stands in for a human reviewer. But it's still only an approximation of human judgment — and next lesson covers what happens when a policy is optimized against that approximation for too long: reward model overoptimization.
